  • Voaters in voatberhoods will get to know each other a bit better

  • Smaller communities will limit the rise of power users
  • Smaller communities will limit the impact of power users over the whole community
  • Trolls will find it more difficult to gain a foothold
  • Brigading will be that much more difficult
  • Smaller communities tend to have more conversations and less attention-whoring GIF posting
  • Smaller communities can build their own personalities

I'm torn on this verdict. While I can see that it might be stifling to certain genres of music (especially ones that use sampling), I can also see it as the rebirth of music that is actually creative. IMHO, a lot of music genres have been stagnant for almost 30 years because simply rehashing rhythms and beats has become so easy/commonplace. Make producers think hard about getting sued and the lazy ones might drop out while the creative ones create something new.

Exactly why it's a good ruling. This will make it much harder for the industry to crank out knock-offs and rehashes constantly.

The challenge in public opinion has to do with how people hear songs differently. It's obvious that Blurred Lines is a total rip-off of Gaye's song yet people claim otherwise because they don't listen to the song the way a musician writing it would.

the main difference between the Blurred Lines debacle, as opposed to songs that are comprised of similar notes or riffs of other documented songs, is that Thicke and Pharrell were in the studio and literally said "Hey, let's write a song that sounds exactly like that Marvin Gaye track." And that's what they did. And there were legal ramifications of course.

It would be interesting if this alters the way artists approach songwriting but I think it's too massive in scope to enforce this. Practically every single song an artist creates has already in part been written by somebody else. You can create your own lyrics and other minor nuances to the song, but every riff / chord progression has already been written in some capacity. So I don't know if this kind of thing can be avoided entirely. It is definitely in interesting conversation though, and I am curious to see the ramifications of this, if any. I would love to see artists make the extra effort to try to ensure their songs are original and creative as possible. That's what music should be about anyways.
